name: Cajonos Zapotec
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Cajonos Zapotec (cajo1238) is not in the catalog. The single stress-titled item, Teodocio Olivares 2009 (MA report, UT Austin; Glottolog files it under zad as 'Betaza'), was already on file with a text layer and was read in full for Chapter 8: it is a first-hand, instrumentally supported description of the San Melchor Betaza variety and states that stress is root-bound and length-driven (root/penultimate primary stress in native disyllables, initial in two-light-syllable roots, final in 3+-syllable words and long-final compounds, Spanish loans keep source stress), with the author calling it preliminary. No catalog record exists to confirm or contradict. The only Cajonos-proper stress statement known (Nellis & Hollenbach 1980, IJAL, reported second-hand by Teodocio as root-initial stress) remains paywalled (doi:10.1086/465639, uchicago 403) and is the high-priority acquisition.

new_statements.quote: The roots or stems always maintain their stress, as shown in (192), and a secondary stress occurs on the affixes. [...] In disyllabic words, primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable, and the syllable can have low, falling, and occasionally high tone. [...] (p.180) I conclude that primary stress placement is associated with vowel length: length determines stress. [...] In disyllabic roots with low and high tone, the first syllable has primary stress if it is a content word; the second syllable, normally an affix, has secondary stress. [...] In roots with two light syllables which can bear any of the phonological tones, the primary stress normally falls on the first syllable. Lastly, in polysyllabic forms, the primary stress falls on the ultimate syllable and the secondary stress on the penultimate.
new_statements.citation: Teodocio Olivares, Amador. 2009. Betaza Zapotec Phonology: Segmental and Suprasegmental Features. MA report, University of Texas at Austin.

In disyllabic roots with low and high tone, the first syllable has primary stress if it is a content word; the second…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress sits on the root/stem: monosyllabic content words are stressed, CV prefixes and particles are unstressed, and suffixes/clitics added to a root carry only secondary stress, so disyllabic (root+affix or disyllabic-root) words are stressed on the penult = root-initial syllable. The author ties placement to vowel length: a long (low/falling-tone) syllable attracts primary stress, so low+falling compounds and tri-/polysyllabic words have primary stress on the long final syllable with secondary stress on the penult; two light syllables default to initial. Spanish loans keep the source stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Affixes and clitics attached to a root bear secondary stress (root keeps primary); in compounds and polysyllabic words with final primary stress, secondary stress falls on the penultimate syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Compounds with low+falling tone and polysyllabic words stress the (long) final syllable rather than the penult; prefix+root disyllables are final-stressed because the root keeps stress; CV particles/prefixes unstressed; loanwords (old and recent) retain the Spanish stressed syllable, even when reduced to monosyllables; stress is not marked in the practical orthography; tone is contrastive (H, L, falling, rising) and only partially correlated with stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in citation forms (field data, Praat); language is tonal with four contrastive tones, stress described as independent of tone in monosyllables and partially correlated (low/falling, longer vowels) in disyllables.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source describes the Zapotec of San Melchor Betaza (Villa Alta district), which the author classes as a Xhon-group dialect alongside the Cajonos towns, Yaganiza, Yalalag, Zoogocho etc.; Glottolog 5.1 files this thesis under cajo1238 (Cajonos Zapotec, iso zad), but it is not San Pedro Cajonos or San Pablo Yaganiza proper. For Cajonos proper the primary phonology is Nellis & Hollenbach 1980 (IJAL), not opened here; Teodocio reports it second-hand as root-initial stress. The thesis notes tonal inventories differ between Betaza (H, L, falling, rising) and San Pedro Cajonos (four tones incl. mid).

new_statements.quote: In disyllabic words, primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable, and the syllable can have low, falling, and occasionally high tone. [...] I conclude that primary stress placement is associated with vowel length: length determines stress. Additionally, stress patterns are partially related to tone. [...] In roots with two light syllables which can bear any of the phonological tones, the primary stress normally falls on the first syllable. Lastly, in polysyllabic forms, the primary stress falls on the ultimate syllable and the secondary stress on the penultimate.
new_statements.citation: Teodocio Olivares, Amador. 2009. Betaza Zapotec Phonology: Segmental and Suprasegmental Features. MA report, University of Texas at Austin, pp. 177 and 180 (Chapter 8, section 8.1).
new_statements.locator: Chapter 8 'Stress', section 8.1 'Stress in native words': p. 177 (PDF p. 187) first quoted sentence; p. 180 (PDF p. 190) summary paragraph; restated in Conclusions p. 187 (PDF p. 197)
new_statements.reading: Betaza (Xhon/Cajonos-group) Zapotec has root-bound, weight-sensitive stress: content roots carry primary stress and CV affixes/particles secondary or none; in root+suffix disyllables stress is root-initial (penultimate), a long or falling-tone heavy syllable attracts primary stress wherever it sits (so many compounds are final-stressed), two-light-syllable roots default to initial stress, and words of three or more syllables take primary stress on the final syllable; Spanish loans keep their source stress. Not a fixed-position system; the closest catalog coding would be weight-sensitive (vowel length) with a root-initial default, and the author flags the analysis as preliminary. Variety caveat: San Melchor Betaza, not San Pedro Cajonos/Yaganiza.
